title: Remote Services: Cloud Services
summary: This sub-technique covers using valid, synchronised, or federated identities to sign in to a cloud control plane rather than to a server on the corporate network. Because the same directory account may be federated to the provider, an intruder who steals one set of credentials can authenticate to the web console, the command line interface, or the provider's API, then manage resources, read storage, or create new identities. Telemetry lives with the provider rather than on a local host, so the useful evidence is in sign-in and audit logs: source address, client application, conditional access outcome, and the management actions that follow. Separating an attacker from a travelling administrator depends on geography, device, user agent, and the sequence of operations. An application access token can replace a password entirely, which removes the usual interactive sign-in from the picture.

beginner.definition: Cloud services are computing resources that a company rents from a provider. Many companies link their normal work accounts to these services, so one login opens both. Remote access to cloud services means signing in as a normal user and then managing things there. This happens through a web page or a command tool.
beginner.whyItMatters: A single stolen account can reach a whole cloud environment, not just one computer. The attacker may not need malware at all, because the web console is enough. Provider logs often sit in a different place than the logs your team watches. If you never check cloud sign-ins, a break-in there can go unseen for weeks.
howItWorks: The company links its own user directory to the cloud provider, so staff sign in with normal accounts.
With a valid account, a person opens the provider web console or uses a command line tool.
The provider checks the login and then grants the rights that the account has been given.
From there the person can manage resources, read storage, or create new users and keys.
An attacker repeats this from an unusual place or device, often outside working hours.
Some attackers skip the password and use an application access token instead.
beginner.example: Imagine an office building where one master card opens every door. The same card opens your own room and the building manager's office. If someone copies that card, they walk in through the front door. No alarm sounds, because the guard only checks that the card is valid. Cloud services work like this when company and cloud accounts are joined.
takeaways: Cloud break-ins are recorded in provider sign-in and audit logs, not on your own servers.
Watch for logins from new places, new devices, or unusual times of day.
Application tokens can bypass passwords, so review long-lived credentials as well.

objectives: Explain what federated and synchronised cloud identities are.
Describe how an attacker uses a valid account to reach a cloud control plane.
Identify the provider log sources that record cloud sign-ins and management actions.
Explain why application access tokens change the detection picture.
Describe how to tell an unusual cloud session from a normal travelling administrator.
